title: Climate Resilient Agriculture: A Plan for Filipino Farms Against Typhoons, Floods, Drought and Heat
metaTitle: Climate Resilient Agriculture: A Plan for Filipino Farms
metaDescription: Climate resilient agriculture for Filipino farmers: know your farm's hazards, plant around them, pick tolerant varieties, spread your risk and keep records.
keywords: climate change and agriculture in the Philippines
excerpt: Climate resilient agriculture means farming so that a bad season costs you less and you recover faster. For a Filipino farm, that means knowing which typhoons, floods, dry spells and heat waves hit your town, planting so the crop meets them at its strongest, choosing tolerant varieties, spreading your risk across crops and keeping records for insurance and loans. anee.io reads twenty years of your town's weather and every storm, flood and drought since 2005, so your plan starts from your own farm's history.

blocks.text:
Typhoons, floods, El Nino droughts and hotter days are part of farming in the Philippines. No farm can stop them. But two neighbors can face the same storm and come out of it very differently, because one planned for it and one did not.

That difference is what people mean by resilience. A resilient farm still has bad seasons. It simply loses less in them, saves some of the harvest every time and gets back to planting faster.
What climate resilient agriculture means for a small farm

items: **Know your hazards.** Which months bring typhoons to your town, which lots flood and how often the rains fail.
**Plant around them.** Set the season so the weakest stages miss the riskiest weeks.
**Choose tolerant crops and varieties.** Some rice survives days under water, and some crops shrug off drought.
**Spread the risk.** Several crops, staggered planting and some livestock keep one disaster from taking everything.
**Guard soil and water.** Organic matter, drainage and water storage carry the farm through extremes.
**Keep records and a cushion.** Receipts and harvest records support insurance claims and loans after a loss.

blocks.text: Step one: know the hazards of your own farm

General advice about the climate is not enough, because hazards differ from town to town. A lot in Cagayan meets more typhoons than a lot in Mindanao. A low field near a river floods when an upland field only gets wet.

So start with your own record. List the storms, floods and dry spells of the last ten years, the months they came and what each one cost you. Then mark which lots flooded and which dried out first. That list tells you where to change the plan.
Step two: plant around the riskiest weeks

Every crop has a weak stage. For rice, it is flowering and grain filling. For corn, it is tasseling and silking. So the planting date decides whether those weeks meet a typhoon, a dry spell or a heat wave.

In typhoon areas, plant so the harvest comes before the stormiest months. In El Nino years, plant early and pick a shorter variety. Our guides to the [best time to plant rice](/blog/best-time-to-plant-rice-philippines) and to [El Nino and La Nina farming tips](/blog/el-nino-la-nina-farming-tips) go deeper.
Step three: choose crops and varieties that tolerate the weather

For flood prone fields, submergence tolerant rice like NSIC Rc 194 (Submarino 1) can survive about two weeks under water and still give a harvest. For dry, rainfed fields, NSIC Rc 192 (Sahod Ulan 1) and NSIC Rc 480 (GSR 8) carry drought tolerance. Our [rice variety finder](/rice-varieties) lists each one.

For lots that dry out every year, switch part of the farm to [drought resistant crops](/blog/drought-resistant-crops) like mongo, peanut or sorghum. Also, choose shorter, sturdier rice where strong winds are common, because tall palay falls over first, as our guide on [lodging in rice](/blog/lodging-in-rice) shows.
Step four: spread the risk and protect soil and water

A farm with one crop planted on one day can lose everything in one storm. A farm with two or three crops, planted a few weeks apart, rarely does. Our pages on a [staggered planting schedule](/blog/staggered-planting-schedule) and the [integrated farming system](/blog/integrated-farming-system) show how to set this up.

Then look after the soil. Compost and crop residue help it hold water in drought and drain better after floods. Keep canals and drains clear before the rainy season, and if you can, dig a small farm pond to store water for the dry months.

blocks.title: Records are part of resilience
blocks.text: After a disaster, insurers, lenders and aid programs ask what you planted, when and what you lost. A farmer with dated records and receipts gets help faster. Our guide to [farm records for loans and insurance](/blog/farm-records-for-loans-and-insurance) shows what to keep.

items.q: What is climate resilient agriculture in simple words?
items.a: Farming so that typhoons, floods, droughts and heat cost you less and you recover faster. It mixes good timing, tolerant varieties, spread out risk, healthy soil and good records.

items.q: Is climate resilient agriculture the same as climate smart agriculture?
items.a: They overlap. Climate smart agriculture also aims to cut farm emissions. For a small Filipino farm, the first goal of both is the same: a harvest that survives a bad season.
Submergence tolerant varieties like NSIC Rc 194 (Submarino 1) can live through about two weeks under water. Check our rice variety finder for the ones suited to your area.

items.q: How can an app help my farm face the climate?
items.a: anee.io reads your town's weather and hazard record, picks a safer planting window, tracks typhoons near your lots and keeps the records you need after a loss. Anee answers your questions in Tagalog or English.
